"Long in the tooth" is an idiom that simply means old or getting old. When you say someone or something is "long in the tooth," you are saying they are aging, often with the quiet suggestion that they may be past their best days or showing the natural wear of time.

Example: "He's a bit long in the tooth to be playing professional football."
That sentence means: He is too old to still be playing professional football.

This idiom was born from the world of horses, and once you understand this, the phrase will make perfect and permanent sense in your mind.

Historically, people bought and sold horses regularly, and a horse's age was one of the most important things a buyer needed to know. An old horse cannot work as hard, run as fast, or last as long as a young one. So buyers needed a reliable way to check a horse's age — especially because dishonest sellers might lie about it.

The answer was in the horse's mouth.

As a horse ages, its gums slowly recede (pull back and shrink). Because the gums are pulling away, more and more of each tooth becomes exposed and visible. So the teeth of an older horse look longer than the teeth of a young horse — even though the teeth haven't actually grown. It's the gums that have shrunk, giving the illusion of longer teeth.

So when a knowledgeable buyer opened a horse's mouth and saw very long-looking teeth, they immediately knew: this horse is old. A young horse, on the other hand, has short-looking teeth because its gums are full and healthy, covering more of each tooth.

Over time, people started applying this horse-inspection logic to humans and other things, using it as a casual, slightly humorous way to say "old."

The short version of the origin: Old horse = long-looking teeth. Long teeth = old. "Long in the tooth" = old.

This is also why another famous idiom exists: "Don't look a gift horse in the mouth." That phrase warns you not to examine a gift too critically — because if someone gives you a horse for free, it's rude and ungrateful to immediately check its teeth (i.e., judge its age and value). Both idioms share the same historical root.

This is an important nuance to understand.

"Long in the tooth" is not a harsh insult. It sits somewhere between a neutral observation and a gentle, slightly humorous comment. It often carries a tone of mild affection or light teasing rather than cruelty.

Think of it this way — if a 60-year-old uncle tries to do a back-flip at a family party, someone might chuckle and say, "He's getting a little long in the tooth for that!" It's not mean-spirited. It's fond and a little funny.

That said, context always matters. If someone says it coldly or dismissively — "She's too long in the tooth for this job" — it can feel unkind. Use your judgment based on the situation and the speaker's tone.

You can also use it about yourself, and when you do, it usually sounds self-aware and charming:
"I'm a bit long in the tooth to be staying up until 3 AM!"
What Can Be "Long in the Tooth"?

This is one of the most flexible things about this idiom. It's not only used for people. It can describe:

People: "The professor is getting long in the tooth, but his lectures are still brilliant."

Animals: "That old dog is long in the tooth, but he still runs to the door every time I come home."

Objects (cars, machines, technology, buildings): "That laptop is getting long in the tooth — it can barely run modern software."

Organizations, ideas, or systems: "Some people think the traditional 9-to-5 workday is getting a bit long in the tooth in the modern world."

The common thread in all of these is the same: whatever is being described has been around a long time and is showing its age.

When you call something "long in the tooth," you're not just saying it's old — you're adding a quiet layer of meaning underneath. You're suggesting:

  • It has been around for a long time.
  • It may be struggling to keep up with newer, younger, or fresher things.
  • It still exists and functions, but perhaps not at its peak.

It's the difference between saying "That car is old" and "That car is getting long in the tooth." The second version paints a more vivid picture — you can almost see the old car sputtering along, a little worn, a little tired, but still going.

• "The actor is a little long in the tooth to be playing a teenage hero, but somehow it works."
  • "Our company's software is getting long in the tooth — we need to upgrade."
  • "I know I'm long in the tooth for this kind of adventure, but I still want to try."
  • "The tradition is long in the tooth, but people still love it."
  • "Even long in the tooth, she danced with more grace than anyone half her age."

MeaningOld; aging; past one's prime
OriginHorse's gums recede with age, making teeth look longer — so long teeth = old horse
ToneGently humorous, mildly affectionate; not usually harsh
Used forPeople, animals, objects, systems, ideas — anything that ages
FeelingSuggests something has been around a long time and may be struggling to keep up

The beauty of this idiom is its story. Every time you hear or use "long in the tooth," you can picture a wise old horse, mouth open, with teeth that have seen better days — and the meaning will never leave you.
